accuracy.evidence: Checked every number the lab and items produce: 13 loose cubes bundle into 1 ten and 3 ones; the read rounds are 2 tens 4 ones = 24, 1 ten 7 ones = 17 and 4 tens 1 one = 41; the swaps take 1 ten 14 ones to 2 tens 4 ones (24 both times) and 2 tens 11 ones to 3 tens 1 one (31); the chart targets 17, 30 and 10 decompose correctly; and t*10+o, n-10, t*10 and 10+o hold at every corner. The 1.NBT.B.2a, 2b and 2c wording matches the published standard.

misconceptions.evidence: Built around the documented first-grade place-value errors: counting a ten rod as one unit (2 rods and 4 cubes read as 6), reversing the digits (17 written as 71), believing more pieces means a bigger amount (15 ones beats 2 tens), thinking cubes are lost or gained in an exchange, and reading the 0 in 10 or 30 as nothing instead of a zero that holds the ones place.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagbundle is about unitising and exchange: loose cubes physically fill a ten-slot tray and turn into a single rod, ten ones must be circled one by one before they become a ten in the tens column, and the tens-and-ones chart regroups itself when the ones reach ten. No other flag lab bundles units into a new unit, and the 30% shingle gate passed against all other labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees ten singles become one rod before the word ten is defined, then has to read rods as tens to answer, watches the running total stay at 24 and 31 while the grouping changes, builds 30 and discovers no ones are needed, and in the compare step must choose 1 ten over 9 ones, so each rule is met in action before the text states it.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions each carry a tempting wrong answer: 4 (counting the rod as 1) or 31 (digits reversed) for 1 rod and 3 cubes; 10 fewer cubes after a swap; and 30 or 3 ones to make 30. After each task the completion line repeats the learner's guess and why the lab showed otherwise.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with every wrong option tagged to its own message: rod counted as 1, digits the wrong way round, a ten as 1 or 100 ones, the whole number given as the tens, the swapped ten lost, too many ones swapped, more pieces read as more, and the 0 read as nothing or as 0 tens. Option order rotates every question.

readability.evidence: The kid paragraphs score about grade -0.7 on learn/readability.py, with sentences about snapping cubes into a stick; lab prompts stay under fifteen short words. The adult notes score about grade 6.3 and name unitising, base-ten blocks, exchanging (regrouping), zero holding a place and the 1.NBT.B.2 strands precisely.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence is a concrete action or a fact about tens and ones; the adult paragraphs are a standards reference, the unitising idea, a list of named mistakes and a summary of what each lab step does. The familyTip is a straw-bundling game with a question to ask. The filler scan found nothing.

mobile.evidence: Checked screenshots at 390 px in light and dark: the young layout puts 56 px buttons (Put a cube in, Circle a one, + ten, + one, Left side, Right side) under the canvas, the ten rods and rows of five ones fit inside each half of the canvas, the tens column is capped at five rods so it never overflows, and any tap on the canvas in step 1 bundles the next cube.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin, the canvas aria-label updates with each spoken line (running counts of cubes, tens and ones), predictions and the Challenge use labelled button groups with a polite live status, and the walkthrough's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
